1: Released in 2019/2020 and later named Billboard's No. 1 Hot 100 song of all time (Nov 2021), it spent a record 88+ weeks on the Hot 100 and became the first song to cross 5 billion Spotify streams; built on 1980s-style synth-pop and a driving 172 BPM tempo.
2: Lead single from 21 (2011), it won Grammy Awards for Record and Song of the Year and topped charts in over 10 countries, blending blues, soul and pop-rock with gospel-tinged backing vocals and handclap percussion.
3: Lead single from 1989 (2014), marking Swift's full pivot from country to pop; produced by Max Martin and Shellback, it debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 and features a prominent horn-driven hook and spoken-word bridge.
4: From Thriller (1983), its iconic basswork and Jackson's own moonwalk debut on the Motown 25 TV special made it a defining music-video moment; it topped the Hot 100 for seven weeks and won two Grammys.
5: From Future Nostalgia (2020), the DaBaby remix became one of the longest-charting Hot 100 hits of the early 2020s; its disco-funk bassline and nu-disco production nodded explicitly to late-1970s dance music.
6: Second single from debut album Oracular Spectacular (2008), recorded at Tarbox Road Studios with producer Dave Fridmann; it became MGMT's first ARIA and RIANZ chart hit and placed 2nd in Triple J's Hottest 100 of 2008.
7: From debut album Lungs (2009), it features handclap-driven percussion and harp, and became a UK top-40 hit after being used in the 2010 Winter Olympics ad campaign and widely in film/TV trailers.
8: Breakout 2010 single later included on Torches (2011); its upbeat synth-pop groove contrasts with dark lyrics about a school shooter, a juxtaposition that sparked public debate upon its mainstream radio success.
9: Originally released in 2010 featuring vocals by Lovefoxxx (CSS) and co-produced with Daft Punk's Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo; it opened the 2011 film Drive's title sequence and went Diamond in France and Gold in Germany.
10: Featured prominently in the 2011 film Drive, this collaboration between French producer College and Canadian duo Electric Youth is widely credited with helping spark the modern synthwave revival of the early 2010s.
11: From the Trilogy compilation (2015), accompanied by an animated music video by writer/director Seth Ickerman; its aggressive, distorted synth-metal hybrid sound became a flagship track of the darksynth subgenre.
12: Released in 2011, it samples Etta James's 1962 vocal from 'Something's Got a Hold on Me' and became one of the defining big-room progressive house anthems of the early 2010s EDM boom.
13: Released in 2011 from Guetta's Nothing but the Beat, Sia originally wrote the topline for her own use before giving it to Guetta; it reached No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart and became a staple of EDM radio crossover.
14: Released in 2013 when Garrix was only 17, this big-room house instrumental topped the UK Singles Chart and Beatport charts, and is widely credited with launching his international festival career.
15: Lead single from True (2013), notable for fusing folk-acoustic guitar and Aloe Blacc's soulful vocal with four-on-the-floor EDM production; it topped charts in over 20 countries and reshaped mainstream dance-pop.
16: Released August 21, 2020 as BTS's first fully English-language single, written and produced by David Stewart and Jessica Agombar in a 1970s disco-pop style; it debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100.
17: Released in 2012, it became the first YouTube video to reach 1 billion views and held the all-time most-viewed spot for years; its satirical lyrics mock Seoul's affluent Gangnam district, and its horse-riding dance went globally viral.
18: Title track of the 2019 EP of the same name, produced by Teddy Park; its music video broke YouTube's 24-hour debut-view record at the time, and the brass-stab hook became one of the group's signature sounds.
19: Released in 2016, this track won Song of the Year at the 2016 Melon Music Awards and its 'Shy shy shy' line (adapted from a Korean idiom) became a nationwide catchphrase, cementing TWICE as a dominant crossover act.
20: Released in 2017, the Justin Bieber remix became the first Spanish-language No. 1 on the Hot 100 since 'Macarena,' tied Mariah Carey's 16-week record atop the chart, and its original video became the most-viewed YouTube video of all time with over 3 billion views.
21: From the 2004 album Barrio Fino, widely considered the song that broke reggaeton into mainstream international markets; it popularized the dembow riddim globally and remains one of the genre's most sampled/referenced tracks.
22: Released in 2019, it interpolates the chorus melody of Snow's 1992 reggae-dancehall hit 'Informer,' bridging reggaeton with 1990s dancehall nostalgia; it reached No. 1 on Billboard's Latin charts and surpassed 1 billion YouTube views.
23: Opening track of Let It Bleed (1969), recorded during the Vietnam War/Altamont era; Merry Clayton's uncredited-at-first wailing guest vocal on 'rape, murder' became one of rock's most famous backing vocal performances.
24: Lead single from Superunknown (1994); won the Grammy for Best Hard Rock Performance and its surreal, melting-suburbia music video became an MTV fixture, helping define the grunge era's darker psychedelic turn.
25: Closing centerpiece of the 'Concerto for a Rainy Day' suite on Out of the Blue (1977); layered with a 30-voice vocal choir, vocoder effects, and full orchestra, it has had a long afterlife via film/TV use and a 2000s streaming resurgence.
26: Opener of Elephant (2003); the famous bassline riff was actually a guitar run through an octave pedal (no bassist in the duo), and its stadium-chant hook made it a worldwide sporting-event anthem.
27: First single from debut album Ten (1991); part of Eddie Vedder's unplanned 'Momma-Son' trilogy about a mother's affair revealed to her son, it became an unintentional fan-crowd anthem despite its dark lyrical origin.
28: Title track of the 1986 album widely considered a thrash-metal landmark; features a tempo that shifts from blistering ~212 BPM thrash riffing to a slower, melodic clean-guitar middle section before returning to full speed.
29: Closing track of Reign in Blood (1986), produced by Rick Rubin; its thunderstorm intro and accelerating, tempo-shifting structure made it one of thrash metal's most covered and sampled songs.
30: Closing track of The Number of the Beast (1982); narrated from the perspective of a man awaiting execution, it doubles tempo in its back half and is frequently cited as one of Maiden's finest compositions.
31: Lead single from Toxicity (2001); its lyrics referencing suicide/self-destruction drew controversy and radio pulls after 9/11 just weeks after release, yet it became the band's signature crossover hit with its jarring tempo and dynamic shifts.
32: Opening piece of Ambient 1: Music for Airports (1978), the album that effectively coined the term 'ambient music'; built from tape loops of piano notes of differing lengths, designed to be 'as ignorable as it is interesting.'
33: Released 2011 in collaboration with the British Academy of Sound Therapy; built on a steady 60 BPM pulse that mimics resting heart rate, widely publicized as 'the most relaxing song ever recorded.'
34: Opening track of Agaetis byrjun (1999); sung in Icelandic/invented 'Hopelandic' vocables with Jonsi's bowed-guitar textures, it gained wider exposure after being featured in the film Vanilla Sky (2001).
35: An eight-minute musique-concrete sound collage on The Beatles (White Album, 1968), assembled largely by John Lennon and Yoko Ono from looped tape fragments; it remains the most divisive, avant-garde track the band ever released on a studio album.
36: Ten-minute closing track of Suicide's self-titled 1977 debut; a pioneering minimal-synth/proto-industrial piece narrating a factory worker's murder-suicide, punctuated by Alan Vega's harrowing screams over a relentless drum-machine pulse.
37: Nearly 10-minute title track of Bowie's final album (released Jan 8, 2016, two days before his death); recorded with jazz musicians from Donny McCaslin's quartet, blending free-jazz saxophone with electronic production in a multi-part suite structure.
38: Third movement of the Suite bergamasque for solo piano, composed around 1890 and revised before its 1905 publication; marked 'Andante tres expressif,' it became one of the most recognizable Impressionist piano pieces through countless film and media placements.
39: Premiered in Vienna in December 1808 on the same concert as the Sixth Symphony; its iconic four-note opening motif drives the work from a stormy C-minor opening to a jubilant C-major finale.
40: Ballet score premiered in Paris on May 29, 1913, under Nijinsky's choreography; its jagged rhythms and dissonant harmonies famously provoked a near-riot in the audience and is now regarded as a founding work of musical modernism.
41: Composed in 1978 for violin (or cello) and piano just before Part emigrated from Soviet Estonia; written in his signature 'tintinnabuli' style of slow triadic arpeggios, it has become a widely licensed staple of film and television scoring.
42: A 40-part motet for eight 5-voice choirs composed around 1570, likely for Elizabeth I's court; its spatial antiphonal effects, with voices entering in sequence across 40 independent parts, make it one of the most technically ambitious works of the Renaissance.
43: Composed around 1638 for the Sistine Chapel choir to be sung only during Holy Week; the Vatican banned transcription of the piece until the 14-year-old Mozart reportedly transcribed it from memory in 1770, famous for its soaring top-C soprano line.
44: Composed in 1994, setting a Latin responsorial Nativity text; it has become one of the most frequently performed American choral works of the late 20th century, prized for its slow-moving modal harmonies and luminous close voicings.
45: Lead single from the 8 Mile soundtrack (2002), it became Eminem's first US Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 and held the top spot for 12 weeks, later winning the 2003 Academy Award for Best Original Song.
46: From Illmatic (1994), produced by DJ Premier using samples of Donald Byrd's 'Flight Time' and Joe Chambers' 'Mind Rain'; widely cited as one of the greatest single verses in hip hop history.
47: Lead single from DAMN. (2017), produced by Mike WiLL Made-It; won the 2018 Grammy for Best Rap Performance and its stark black-and-white video won Best Music Video.
48: Released in 1979 and widely credited as hip hop's first mainstream hit; its groove re-plays (rather than samples) Chic's 'Good Times' bassline, leading Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards to sue and win songwriting credit.
49: From To Pimp a Butterfly (2015), produced by Pharrell Williams and Sounwave; its 'we gon' be alright' hook became a chanted rallying cry at Black Lives Matter protests nationwide.
50: Debut single from Ready to Die (1994), built on a sample of Mtume's 1983 'Juicy Fruit'; autobiographically traces Biggie's rise from poverty in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn to rap stardom.
51: Lead single from Beyonce's solo debut Dangerously in Love (2003), its horn hook samples The Chi-Lites' 'Are You My Woman (Tell Me So)'; won two Grammys including Best R&B Song.
52: From FanMail (1999), hit No. 1 on the Hot 100 and won two Grammys; it popularized 'scrub' as mainstream slang for an unambitious man chasing women he can't afford to impress.
53: A nearly 10-minute two-part epic from Channel Orange (2012) that shifts tempo partway through, moving from an ancient-Egypt myth narrative to a modern strip-club scene, and featuring a guitar solo from John Mayer.
54: Lead single from Kaleidoscope Dream (2012), written and self-produced by Miguel; won the 2013 Grammy for Best R&B Song and became his second No. 1 on the R&B/Hip-Hop chart.
55: From the album 4 (2011), a tribute to 1980s R&B whose outro climbs through four consecutive key changes (C to E) -- a feat that reportedly inspired the album's title.
56: Franklin's 1967 reworking of Otis Redding's song added the iconic 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T' spell-out and 'sock it to me' backing vocals, turning it into a feminist and civil-rights anthem; won her first two Grammys and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame.
57: Title track released January 1971; Gaye self-produced it over Motown founder Berry Gordy's initial objections, addressing war, poverty, and police brutality. The album is ranked No. 6 on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums list.
58: Recorded in December 1963 and released as a single in December 1964, 11 days after Cooke's death; it became one of the defining anthems of the civil rights movement and is inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
59: From Menagerie (1977), famous for Withers sustaining a note for about 18 seconds near the end, long cited as one of the longest held notes in a Top 40 hit; the 1988 'Sunshine Mix' reissue reached No. 4 in the UK.
60: Lead single from her 1997 debut Baduizm, which hit No. 2 on the Billboard 200; the song won Best Female R&B Vocal Performance at the 1998 Grammys and helped define the emerging neo-soul sound.
61: From Voodoo (2000), won the 2001 Grammy for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance; its single-take, nude music video made D'Angelo an instant sex symbol, a reaction he later said complicated his relationship to his own music.
62: Lead single from New Amerykah Part Two (2010); its guerrilla-shot video, filmed at Dallas's Dealey Plaza and showing Badu gradually disrobing, led to a disorderly conduct charge against her.
63: A 1969 reworking of an 18th-century hymn that unexpectedly crossed over to pop radio, reaching No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 in the UK; won the 1970 Grammy for Best Soul Gospel Performance.
64: Released in 1996 on Adoration: Live in Atlanta with Vision, it became one of the most widely performed songs in Black church worship and was later covered a cappella by Destiny's Child in their 2007 'Gospel Medley'.
65: Lead single from Hello Fear (2011), it reached No. 85 on the Hot 100 (Franklin's first Hot 100 entry in six years) and won the 2012 Grammy for Song of the Year (Gospel) plus Dove and Stellar Awards.
66: From Future's self-titled 2017 album, built around a flute sample from Tommy Butler's 'Prison Song'; went RIAA gold and spawned the viral #MaskOffChallenge of musicians recreating the flute line.
67: From Culture (2017), it hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 2017 -- the first chart-topper for both Migos and Lil Uzi Vert -- and helped popularize the triplet-flow ad-lib style across pop culture.
68: Emo-trap single released in 2017, produced by TM88 and JW Lucas; peaked at No. 7 on the Hot 100, certified Diamond by the RIAA, and became a defining anthem of the 'emo rap' wave with its nihilistic 'push me to the edge' hook.
69: From 1959's Time Out, built on an unusual 5/4 time signature with Paul Desmond's alto sax melody; became a surprise Top 40 hit despite its odd meter.
70: Opening track of 1959's Kind of Blue, the best-selling jazz album of all time; pioneered modal jazz with Paul Chambers' bass intro answered by horns.
71: From her 1965 album I Put a Spell on You, originally written for the 1964 musical The Roar of the Greasepaint; dramatic horn swells made it one of the most sampled vocal jazz tracks ever.
72: Composed by Monk in 1944, it's the most recorded jazz standard in history; Miles Davis's 1957 version on 'Round About Midnight is a landmark recording.
73: From the 2004 Samurai Champloo Music Record: Departure soundtrack; built around a harp/flute sample, it became a defining lofi hip-hop touchstone after Nujabes' 2010 death, reissued in 2024 for the anime's 20th anniversary.
74: Instrumental chillhop cut from Jinsang's 2016 album Life., built on a mellow looped piano and soft boom-bap drums; a staple of lofi hip-hop study/relax playlists.
75: By Finnish producer Idealism (Lassi Kotamaki), who cites Nujabes as a core influence; blends piano-led chillhop with a soft vocal hook from brillion, one of his most-streamed tracks.
76: Originally acoustic on 1964's Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.; producer Tom Wilson secretly overdubbed electric guitar, bass and drums in 1965, and the new version hit #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1966.
77: From 1963's The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, it became a defining civil-rights-era anthem; Peter, Paul and Mary's cover version reached #2 on the Billboard Hot 100 that same year.
78: From 1970's Ladies of the Canyon, its environmentalist refrain 'paved paradise, put up a parking lot' made it an enduring protest-folk anthem, later a hit cover for Counting Crows in 2002.
79: From the 2007 debut For Emma, Forever Ago, recorded largely alone by Justin Vernon in an isolated Wisconsin cabin; Birdy's 2011 cover later became a bigger chart hit than the original.
80: 1973 #1 Billboard Hot Country Songs hit, inspired by a flirtatious bank teller Parton once encountered; its fingerpicked guitar riff is one of country music's most recognizable intros.
81: From 1990's No Fences, it hit #1 on Hot Country Songs and became a honky-tonk/karaoke standard, famous for its rowdy shout-along chorus.
82: From 2013's Southeastern, written about Isbell getting sober and falling in love with now-wife Amanda Shires; became a #1 country hit as a 2020 Morgan Wallen cover.
83: 1967 duet that won the Grammy for Best Country Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group; built on a bickering call-and-response narrative between the two real-life spouses.
84: From 2020's Made in Lagos; after a Justin Bieber remix, it became one of the first Nigerian pop songs to crack the Billboard Hot 100 top 10, in 2021.
85: From 2018's Outside, its title referencing Kanye West's album; became a global viral hit and was later interpolated into Beyonce's 'Already'.
86: From 2022's Love Damini, sampling Toni Braxton's 'He Wasn't Man Enough'; a heartbreak anthem that topped multiple African streaming charts.
87: From 2022's Rave & Roses; its 2023 Selena Gomez remix reached the Billboard Hot 100 top 5, making it one of the most-streamed Afrobeats songs ever.
88: The beloved live version is from 1975's Live! album, recorded at London's Lyceum Theatre; the Jamaican patois title translates to 'woman, don't cry'.
89: UB40's 1983 reggae reworking of Neil Diamond's 1967 song; a 1988 re-release hit #1 on both the UK and US Billboard Hot 100.
90: 1969 single that is a foundational rocksteady/early-reggae track; featured in the 1972 film The Harder They Come and later covered by The Clash.
91: From 1978's Kaya, it reached #9 on the UK singles chart, one of Marley's biggest UK hits, with a smooth lovers-rock-leaning groove.
92: Written by Antonio Carlos Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes; the 1964 recording won the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year and was inspired by a teenage girl, Helo Pinheiro, who walked past a Rio cafe.
93: Composed by Jobim and Newton Mendonca in 1959; the title means 'out of tune,' and Gilberto's hushed vocal over syncopated guitar helped define the bossa nova style.
94: Written by Jorge Ben in 1963; Mendes's 1966 version became a US Top 40 crossover hit, and was reinterpreted with the Black Eyed Peas in 2006.
95: From her Grammy-nominated 2013 album Traces of You, co-written with Nitin Sawhney; blends sitar with electronic production.
96: Instrumental opener on the duo's self-titled 2006 breakout album, fusing flamenco fingerstyle guitar with a thrash-metal-derived rhythmic attack, reflecting both musicians' metal-band roots.
97: From 2004's Amassakoul; hypnotic electric guitar 'desert blues' from the Tuareg band whose members were once Malian rebel-fighters-turned-musicians.
98: Breakthrough ballad from George 'Fiji' Veikoso's 1994 debut album Evolution, a cornerstone of the Hawaii-based island-reggae sound he helped pioneer before his death in 2025.
99: From J Boog's 2011 album Backyard Boogie, co-written with Fiji and produced by Don Corleon; the UK's BPI certified it silver more than a decade after release.
100: From Kalani Pe'a's 2016 debut album E Walea, sung entirely in 'olelo Hawai'i; the album won the Grammy for Best Regional Roots Music Album and the Na Hoku Hanohano Award for Contemporary Album of the Year.
